name: Korea under Japanese rule
info: Korea as a colony of the Empire of Japan under the name Chōsen, ruled by a Governor-General in Keijō from the annexation of 1910 until Japan's surrender in 1945, and remembered for forced assimilation, extraction and mass mobilisation.

facts.founder: The Empire of Japan, by the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910 signed by Ye Wanyong and Terauchi Masatake, the first Governor-General of Chōsen
facts.predecessor: Korean Empire, a Japanese protectorate from the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905
facts.successor: Soviet and American occupation zones divided at the 38th parallel (1945), then North and South Korea (1948)

t: Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905, forced Emperor Gojong to abdicate in 1907 and annexed the country by the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910, ruling it through a Governor-General of Chōsen based in Keijō.

Under the theory of Nissen dōsoron the colonial government pursued Japanization, closing Korean newspapers, phasing out all Korean language courses by 1943 and pressing Koreans to take Japanese surnames under the Sōshi-kaimei decrees of 1939.

From 1939 Japan mobilised around 5.4 million Koreans for its war effort; many were moved by force to mines and factories, and women and girls were forced into sexual slavery as "comfort women" for Japanese soldiers.
dyk: The colonial authorities destroyed 85 percent of all the buildings in Gyeongbokgung Palace, and built the Japanese General Government Building on the exact site of its primary building.
ev: On 22 August Japan annexes Korea by the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910, and Terauchi Masatake becomes the first Governor-General of Chōsen
After Emperor Gojong's sudden death, the March First Movement brings an estimated 2 million people to peaceful rallies, which Japan violently suppresses
Independence forces under Kim Chwajin and Hong kill about 1,500 Japanese soldiers at the Battle of Cheongsanri, and the Imperial Japanese Army retaliates with the Gando massacre
The Gwangju Students Independence Movement of 3 November leads to the strengthening of Japanese military rule in 1931
The Korean Patriotic Organization of Kim Ku attempts to assassinate Emperor Hirohito and bombs a military rally in Shanghai
Recruitment of Korean labour for Japan begins, and the Sōshi-kaimei decrees press Koreans to give up their clan-based family names
Japan begins conscripting Korean men into the Imperial Japanese Army and the military industrial sector
Japan surrenders on 15 August, ending 35 years of colonial rule, and Korea is divided at the 38th parallel between American and Soviet forces

sections.foundation:
Japan forced Korea open with the unequal Japan–Korea Treaty of 1876, signed under the gunboat diplomacy of the Ganghwa Island incident. Its agents assassinated Queen Min on 8 October 1895, and after its victories over China in 1894–1895 and over Russia in 1904–1905 it was left the sole regional power. By the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905 Korea became a protectorate ruled through the Resident-General, and the Korean Army was cut from 20,000 to 1,000 men. When Emperor Gojong sent envoys to the Second Peace Conference at The Hague in 1907 to question the protectorate, Japan forced him to relinquish his authority on 19 July 1907, and Sunjong became the last ruler of the Joseon dynasty.

The disbanded troops joined the "righteous armies", peasant militias that fought the Japanese until a scorched-earth campaign drove them into Manchuria and Russia, and on 26 October 1909 Ahn Jung-geun assassinated Ito Hirobumi in Harbin. On 22 August 1910 Ye Wanyong, Prime Minister of Korea, and Terauchi Masatake signed the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910, by which the Emperor of Korea conceded his entire sovereignty to the Emperor of Japan. Terauchi became the first Governor-General of Chōsen, and the years 1910–19 are known as the Military Police Reign Era.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Land Survey Bureau's cadastral surveys recognised ownership only on written proof, so cultivators with traditional rights lost their land, and Japanese individuals and companies such as the Oriental Development Company took over more and more of it. Tenants, all Korean, paid over half their crop in rent, and many left as labourers for Japan or Manchuria. As rice was exported to Japan, per capita rice consumption among Koreans in 1932–1936 fell to half its level of 1912–1916. Japan built railways, ports and roads and, from the late 1920s under Governor-General Kazushige Ugaki, chemical plants, steel mills and munitions works. Economic output rose tenfold from 1910 to 1945, but in 1939 about 94 percent of factory capital was Japanese-owned, and scholars argue that much of the infrastructure was built to extract resources rather than to benefit Koreans.

In 1934 the Japanese in Chōsen numbered about 561,000 of over 21 million people, living largely in segregated districts of the cities. Korea also became a major exporter of opium and narcotics in the 1930s, supplying the opium monopoly of Manchukuo. Christianity grew, from 86,000 Protestants and 79,000 Catholics in 1914 to 168,000 and 147,000 by 1934, and for some Koreans it became an expression of nationalism.
sections.military:
Japan replaced the Korean police with its military police, the Kempeitai, under Akashi Motojiro, and combined the two forces in June 1910. Armed resistance continued from Manchuria and Primorsky Krai: Beom-do Hong's unit won the Battle of Bongodong in June 1920, and forces under Kim Chwajin and Hong killed about 1,500 Japanese soldiers at the Battle of Cheongsanri, after which the Imperial Japanese Army committed the Gando massacre, killing between 5,000 and tens of thousands of Korean civilians. The invasion of Manchuria in 1932 deprived many guerrilla groups of their bases; Kim Il Sung was among the leaders there. The Korean Liberation Army, founded by Kim Ku in Chongqing, fought in China and Burma.

Until 1944 enlistment of Koreans in the Imperial Japanese Army was voluntary, though historians such as Pyo Young-Soo find systematic coercion behind it; from 1944 Korean men were conscripted into the army or the war industries, and about 200,000 were inducted. Of the 5,400,000 Koreans conscripted for labour, about 670,000 were taken to Japan, where 60,000 died; estimates of deaths in Korea and Manchuria range between 270,000 and 810,000. After the war 148 Koreans were convicted of Class B and C war crimes, many of them prison guards.
sections.governance:
Korea was ruled by the Governor-General of Chōsen in Keijō, through 13 provinces. Koreans were nominally granted Japanese citizenship but denied freedom of speech, assembly and an independent press; the Newspaper Act of 1907 and later closures left only government-backed papers until the cultural rule policy after 1919 allowed The Chosun Ilbo and The Dong-A Ilbo, and in 1940 all Korean language newspapers were shut again. The Peace Preservation Law of 1925 banned communist literature throughout the empire.

Policy rested on Nissen dōsoron, the theory that Koreans and Japanese shared mythological ancestors, which justified assimilation without equality. Schools taught the formation of the "Imperial Citizen", and the Regulations for Private Schools of 1911 aimed to undermine Korean institutions thought to breed patriotism. In 1938 policy turned to Naisen ittai; in 1942 the authorities closed the Korean Language Society, and by 1943 all Korean language courses had been phased out. Under the Sōshi-kaimei decrees of 1939 Koreans who kept their names could be refused school places, government services and food rations. From 1937 Koreans were required to worship the Emperor at Shinto shrines; around 2000 Christians who refused were imprisoned and 50 died as martyrs.
sections.impact:
The colonial era shaped the peninsula long after it. The railway network linking Pusan, Seoul and the Chinese border tied Korea's economy to Japan and carried troops to the continent; most of the infrastructure built then was destroyed in the Korean War of 1950–1953. Japan carried out the first modern archaeological excavations in Korea, and the Governor-General's law of 1933 to preserve historical artifacts is the origin of the National Treasures of both South and North Korea. Tens of thousands of cultural artifacts were taken to Japan: the South Korean government counts 75,311 taken from Korea, 34,369 of them in Japan.

Groups of the Korean diaspora date from the period: the Zainichi Koreans descend from about 600,000 who remained in Japan, 43,000 ethnic Koreans were trapped on Sakhalin, and Koreans who had fled to Russia were moved to Central Asia in 1937. Officers who had served Japan, among them Park Chung Hee, went on to careers in post-colonial South Korea. The period remains hotly contested: some conservative Japanese nationalists portray it positively, while scholars such as Mark Caprio argue that Japan's policies systematically excluded most Koreans from the institutions of modernity.
sections.decline:
From 1939 the war turned Korea into a reservoir of labour and soldiers, and the Korean Provisional Government in China, under the presidency of Kim Ku, declared war on Japan and Germany on 10 December 1941. Its Korean Liberation Army prepared to return to the peninsula in the Eagle Project, but the sudden end of the war came first. After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, where many Korean labourers were among the victims, and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945, ending 35 years of colonial rule; Japanese troops remained in the south until mid-September.

American forces under General John R. Hodge arrived on 8 September 1945, while the Soviet Army held the north, and the peninsula was split at the 38th parallel, which led to the foundation of both North and South Korea in 1948. The United States Army Military Government issued a Name Restoration Order on 23 October 1946, and the Shinto shrines were destroyed shortly after liberation. South Korea and Japan had no functional diplomatic relations until the Treaty on Basic Relations of 1965, which declared the treaties of 1910 and before "already null and void".

summary: Korea under Japanese rule was the colony of Chōsen, governed from Keijō by Japanese Governors-General from 1910 to 1945. Japan built railways, ports and industry chiefly to serve its own needs, suppressed the independence movement, sought to erase Korean language and identity, and in the war years mobilised millions of Koreans as labourers, soldiers and sex slaves.
references: Michael E. Robinson, Korea's Twentieth-Century Odyssey: A Short History (University of Hawaii Press, 2007)
Carter J. Eckert, Offspring of Empire: The Koch'ang Kims and the Colonial Origins of Korean Capitalism, 1876–1945 (University of Washington Press, 1996)
Hildi Kang, Under the Black Umbrella: Voices from Colonial Korea, 1910–1945 (Cornell University Press, 2001)
Jun Uchida, Brokers of Empire: Japanese Settler Colonialism in Korea, 1876–1945 (Harvard University Press, 2011)
F. A. McKenzie, Korea's Fight for Freedom (Fleming H. Revell, 1920)

pointDescs.1910: Japan annexes Korea on 22 August, and the Kempeitai and police are combined under military police rule.
pointDescs.1911: The Regulations for Private Schools aim to undermine Korean schools believed to breed patriotism.
pointDescs.1919: The March First Movement draws an estimated 2 million people to peaceful rallies and is violently suppressed; restrictions are then eased under the cultural rule policy.
pointDescs.1920: Independence forces win at Bongodong and Cheongsanri, and the Japanese army answers with the Gando massacre.
pointDescs.1925: The Peace Preservation Law bans communist literature throughout the Empire of Japan, including Korea.
pointDescs.1927: The Government-General sets out the Twelve-Year Railway Plan to carry the mineral resources of northern Korea.
pointDescs.1929: The Gwangju Students Independence Movement breaks out on 3 November.
pointDescs.1931: Japanese military rule is strengthened and press freedom curbed; under Governor-General Kazushige Ugaki heavy industry is built up.
pointDescs.1937: The Northern East Coast Line opens, and Koreans are required to worship the Emperor at Shinto shrines.
pointDescs.1938: Policy turns more aggressively to cultural assimilation under Naisen ittai.
pointDescs.1939: Recruitment of Korean labour for Japan begins and the Sōshi-kaimei decrees take effect; about 94 percent of factory capital is Japanese-owned.
pointDescs.1942: The National Mobilization Law is extended to conscript Korean workers, and the Korean Language Society is closed.
pointDescs.1944: Korean men are conscripted into the army and war industries, while food grain consumption falls 35 percent below that of 1912–1916.
pointDescs.1945: Japan surrenders on 15 August, and American and Soviet forces divide Korea at the 38th parallel.

notes: The power curve measures the colonial regime's hold and extraction, scaled to its wartime peak; the article dates few turning points between 1911 and 1925.

The article contradicts itself on names: 'Koreans were obliged to take Japanese names by 1932' against the Sōshi-kaimei decrees of 1939, and calls the name change both 'officially voluntary' (80% in 1940) and compulsory; I used only 1939 and the penalties it lists.
Land figures conflict (7-8% of arable land under Japanese control in 1910 rising to 52.7% in 1932, against Lee Young-hoon's 'less than 10%', itself contested); left out.
The list of governors-general is out of order and lacks the 1919-1927 term; only Terauchi, Ugaki and Koiso are named.

Comfort women estimates (10,000 to 500,000) are left out of the sections for their range; the article's 'over a year of demonstrations' March First figures (Korean 7,509 killed, Japanese 553) also left out for length.
